title: Why You Shouldn't Ask Misbehaving Students To Explain Themselves s-to-explain-themselves/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that pulling students aside to explain their misbehavior, though a common practice, is a mistake that backfires. Students rarely give a satisfactory answer because, honestly, most misbehave simply because they felt like it in the moment, and forcing them to articulate that leads to denial, arguing, or resentment. He explains that a classroom management plan, not personal interrogation, is meant to hold students accountable without adding friction. Demanding an explanation makes accountability feel personal, prompting students to blame the teacher rather than reflect on their own choice. He concludes that relationships and rapport, not confrontation, give teachers real influence, closing with the memorable line a teacher can use instead: 'You're better than that.'
points: Most students genuinely cannot articulate why they misbehaved beyond 'because I felt like it,' making interrogation pointless and frustrating for both sides.
Demanding an explanation for misbehavior introduces resentment and distrust into a relationship that needs to stay positive.
A classroom management plan, not a personal confrontation, is what should hold students accountable impersonally.
Making discipline personal undermines real accountability because students end up blaming the teacher instead of reflecting.
Strong teacher-student rapport, not confrontation, is what gives a simple phrase like 'You're better than that' its power.
quotes: The truth is, although it is among the most commonly used methods of classroom management, pulling students aside to explain their misbehavior is a mistake.
Most students have a difficult time articulating why they misbehaved, especially because they know you won’t like the answer.
With no acceptable answer to give, students feel cornered and either clam up, argue, or lie about what happened, which makes the teacher more determined than ever to browbeat an answer from them.
Most teachers don’t really want or need to know why students misbehave. They ask because they want them to accept responsibility.
For classroom management to be most effective, your students must view your consequences as something they bring deservedly upon themselves, and for which they’re solely responsible.
It’s your likeability and rapport and the one-on-one connections you make, after all, that give you the leverage and influence to whisper one simple phrase and have it affect them deeply.
